description:
Buscamos personas comprometidas que quieran aportar sus conocimientos y convertir una idea científica en una solución tecnológica, el desafio es Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars

We are looking for committed individuals who wish to contribute their expertise and transform a scientific idea into a technological solution; the chosen challenge is: "Identify Earth locations that are analogous to potential sites for a permanent Moon base or a Mars base."
summary:
PACHA-X: Earth as a laboratory for exploring other worlds.

PACHA-X is an interactive platform that connects regions on Earth with areas on the Moon and Mars to identify potential planetary analogs by comparing geological, geomorphological, mineralogical, and environmental characteristics.

The system allows users to explore planetary surfaces, select regions of interest, and access information organized into four categories: terrain, minerals, environment, and operations. Furthermore, it presents potential terrestrial analogs—such as the Iturralde crater (Araona) in Bolivia and Kīlauea in Hawaii—that enable the study of features and processes relevant to future space missions.

PACHA-X addresses this challenge by transforming scientific and geographic data into an interactive, visual tool that facilitates the identification and comparison of environments. Its significance lies in leveraging the diversity of our planet as a natural laboratory to support research, technological preparation, and the planning of future lunar and Martian exploration missions.
details:
01 What does it do and how does it work? 

• Explore a world. Interactive 3D globes of the Moon and Mars, built from real NASA Trek mosaics (LRO WAC and Viking MDIM 2.1). Zones are highlighted areas: Shackleton, Tycho, Hadley Rille, Jezero, Gale, Meridiani Planum, Valles Marineris and more. 

• Compare by type of analogy. Each zone lists its Earth analogs in four tabs: geomorphological (landforms), mineralogical / geochemical (rocks and chemistry), environmental / habitability (cold, aridity, UV, salinity) and operational (training astronauts, rovers, suits and habitats). Analogs are ordered Bolivia first, then Latin America, then the rest of the world. 

• Read an honest profile of each site. Every analog has its own shareable page: why it resembles the zone, the analogies it fully or partly meets, its breaking point (what it cannot represent), a per-category Reproduces / Breaks analysis, possible training activities with what is measured and their restrictions, an estimated training cost, a location map and its source. 

• Know how established it is. Each analog is labelled Already known (already used or studied as an analog by NASA, another agency or a scientific publication; 33 sites) or Proposed (put forward by our research; 23 sites, all in Bolivia). 

• Estimate the cost of training there. A transparent model computes cost per astronaut or per rover: airfare from Houston, per diem, local transport, altitude acclimatisation days and site fees, based on public U.S. government per-diem rates and published habitat fees. 

02 What benefits does it offer? 

• One place instead of scattered papers. Information about analogs is spread across papers, agency pages and reports. Pacha-X puts it in a single map that a student, teacher, researcher or mission planner can use in minutes. 

• Comparisons with their limits. Showing the breaking point next to every similarity keeps users from over reading an analog. No place on Earth reproduces lunar gravity, the Martian atmosphere or space radiation, and the app says so. 

• Practical planning data. Training ideas plus cost estimates help compare sites. For example, a six-astronaut field trip to a Bolivian site comes to about US$ 12,200–26,400. Grouping all 12 Bolivian field trips into a single expedition cuts that total by 60–80%. 

• Accessible to everyone. The app is free and open, needs no login, works on phones down to 320 px wide, and is available in Spanish and English.

03 What is the intended impact? 

• Put Bolivia on the analog map. The Altiplano combines salt flats (Uyuni, Coipasa), high-altitude hypersaline and thermal lakes (Laguna Verde, Laguna Colorada, Pastos Grandes), volcanoes, rock glaciers and caves within a few hundred kilometres. Pacha-X documents 32 Bolivian sites and makes the case for studying them. 

• Turn "proposed" into "studied". By separating established analogs from proposals, the app gives researchers a clear list of open opportunities. For example, our reference reports flag the hypersaline Cañapa and Chiarkota lagoons as open opportunities for microbiological research. 

• Inspire and teach. Students in Bolivia and Latin America can see that places near them matter for lunar and Martian exploration, and learn planetary science through familiar landscapes. 

• Support better field campaigns. Training ideas, restrictions and cost logic help teams plan field campaigns that are cheaper and more respectful of fragile sites. 

04 Tools, languages, hardware and software 

Area What we used 

Languages TypeScript (strict), SQL (PostgreSQL), HTML / CSS, Python, JavaScript (Node.js scripts) 

Front end React 18, Vite 5, React Router 6, react-globe.gl (three.js / WebGL) for the globes, Leaflet + OpenStreetMap for the Earth location map 

NASA data NASA Trek WMTS mosaics (Moon LRO WAC, Mars Viking MDIM 2.1), NASA Blue Marble and Apollo 17 imagery, NASA Earth Observatory, NASA mission and analog pages 

Data PostgreSQL schema for Supabase with row-level security, versioned migrations and seeds; SQL seeds exported to static JSON (Podman / Docker) so the MVP needs no backend 

Internationalisation Custom native i18n layer: typed UI strings that cannot compile with a missing translation, plus 801 content translations (AI-assisted, reviewed by the team) with a script that flags outdated 

ones 

Hosting and workflow Vercel (static hosting, preview per pull request), Git and GitHub with branch-and-PR reviews 

Other tools Pillow (Python) to generate the logo, favicon and icons; Puppeteer + Firefox for automated browser checks; Claude Code as an AI coding and drafting assistant, with every scientific claim checked against our sources 

Hardware None beyond the team's laptops. The app runs in any modern browser, on desktop or phone. 

05 How is the project creative? 

• The name. Pacha is the Andean (Quechua and Aymara) word for earth, world and time-space; the X stands for exploration. The project looks at other worlds through Andean land. 

• The breaking point as a feature. Most analog lists only say what is similar. We give every site a breaking point and a per-category "reproduces / breaks" analysis, so its limits are part of what the user learns. • Evidence labels. Already known vs. Proposed separates established science from our own research, so users can tell them apart. 

• Science plus logistics. The app links planetary geology with what it would take to send a crew or rover there, through training activities and cost estimates. 

• Immersive but light. 3D globes stitched in the browser from NASA tiles, set in a decorative scene with the Sun and a rotating Earth, all served as a static site.

06 What factors did the team consider? 

• Scientific caution. We follow a written list of claims that need care. Uncertain origins stay open: the Iturralde structure is a possible impact, not a confirmed one, and we do not claim perchlorates at Uyuni without local analysis. Altitude does not equal Martian pressure. 

• Source integrity. Every analog links to a real source. When we lacked one (2 sites), it is shown as "source pending" rather than invented. 

• Evidence levels. Bolivian sites keep the "studied / proposed / suggested" level given in our reference reports. 

• Conservation and safety. Fragile or protected sites (Valle de la Luna, Torotoro, high Andean lakes) carry restrictions; some are recommended for digital or remote study only. Field trips include acclimatisation days and medical checks for altitude. 

• Accessibility. Keyboard navigation, screen-reader labels, reduced-motion support and a layout that works from phones to desktops. 

• Language. Spanish for the local audience and English for the global one, switched in the app itself rather than through browser machine translation. 

• Cost and sustainability. No servers or paid services are needed, so the project can stay online for free. The database schema is ready if the project grows. 

• Image licences. We use only public-domain or Creative Commons photos, with credits. Sites without a suitable photo are marked as pending. 

• Teamwork. Clear ownership of each area, small reviewed pull requests and documentation, so the team could work in parallel.
